findings.paper_title: PCC SWAP Internal Audit Activity Report Sept 2026
findings.headline: 92.5% audit action completion (second best among peer unitary authorities) but 29 actions overdue, 15 severely, concentrated in Corporate Services
findings.detail: The council has completed 387 audit actions with 63 in progress, achieving 92.5% completion rate. Average implementation time of 79 days ranks second among nine unitary authorities benchmarked. However, 29 actions remain overdue as at August 2026, with 15 more than 91 days overdue. Critically, these overdue actions are concentrated in Corporate Services, indicating that implementation challenges are localized to financial and administrative functions rather than spread across all services.
findings.matters: Overall peer-relative performance indicates good management quality and responsiveness, but concentration of lag in Corporate Services (finance/administration) signals specific execution constraints in financially critical functions
findings.figures: 387 completed actions, 63 in progress, 92.5% completion rate, 79 days average implementation (2nd best of 9 peer councils), 29 overdue actions, 15 more than 91 days late
findings.quote: continued focus is required on the 29 overdue actions, particularly those that are significantly overdue and the concentration of outstanding actions within Corporate Services.

findings.paper_title: PCC SWAP Internal Audit Activity Report Sept 2026
findings.headline: All completed audits rated reasonable or substantial assurance; no high corporate risks or limited/no assurance opinions identified
findings.detail: Of 6 audits completed with control opinions, 1 received substantial assurance (fraud prevention) and 5 received reasonable assurance (budget setting, expenses, housing rents, and grants). No audits received limited or no assurance ratings. The report states there are currently no areas of high corporate risk requiring escalation.
findings.matters: Indicates the council has effective governance and control arrangements across audited areas, providing baseline confidence that the control environment is functioning
findings.figures: 1 substantial (17%), 5 reasonable/certified (83%), 0 limited, 0 no assurance, 0 Priority 1 fundamental actions
findings.quote: There are currently no areas of high corporate risk or other significant matters arising from Internal Audit's work that require escalation to the Governance and Audit Committee.

findings.headline: Twelve member interests in live directorships and trusteeships were not declared in the register
findings.detail: The audit identified 12 interests held by 9 members that had not been declared in the register of interests, relating to active trusteeships or directorships during 2025-26. The current member declaration process relies on email reminders with no confirmation of active review when amendments are not made. The auditor has recommended more robust formal declaration procedures with implementation due 31 May 2027.
findings.matters: Undeclared interests in external organizations create risks around conflicts of interest and decision-making integrity in a public sector body.
findings.figures: 12 interests; 9 members
findings.quote: We also identified 12 interests of 9 members which had not been declared in the register of interests which related to live Trusteeship or Directorships during 2025-26.

findings.headline: Council lacks complete formal agreement for Funded Nursing Care pooled budget with health board
findings.detail: The council does not have a complete Section 33 formal agreement for the Funded Nursing Care pooled budget with its health board partner. This creates a control weakness with no contractual footing for the arrangement and creates dispute risk if disagreements arise. The auditor has recommended the partners review and update the agreement, with implementation due 30 November 2026.
findings.matters: Pooled budgets involve shared spending commitments and potential disputes over contributions or liabilities, so without a complete formal agreement, the council's obligations and dispute resolution processes are unclear.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: The Authority has not been able to provide us with a complete S33 agreement for the Funded Nursing Care to support the 2025-26 Pooled Budget. This apparent lack of a formal footing for the Pooled Budget arrangements and the lack of understanding of these arrangements is a potential control weakness, particularly if a dispute should arise between the partners.

findings.headline: New payment system created accounting risk for creditors through missing purchase order data
findings.detail: The council's new payment system did not contain relevant purchase order records, creating problems with payments made after year-end. Combined with a £6.0 million reduction in the creditors balance, this raised a risk that creditors could be materially incomplete. Audit testing with expanded sample sizes found no actual misstatement, but the issue reflects control gaps in system implementation.
findings.matters: System implementation issues affecting creditors and payment processing indicate potential risks to cash management, payables accuracy, and financial reporting reliability.
findings.figures: £6.0 million
findings.quote: We were made aware of problems making payments after the year-end, as the new system did not have the relevant purchase orders present. This, coupled with a reduction of £6.0 million in the creditors balance included in the accounts for 2025-26 could indicate that the creditors balance was materially incomplete.

findings.headline: Audit identified and corrected three material asset misclassifications totaling £8.954 million
findings.detail: Three material asset misclassifications were identified during the audit: a £5.499 million asset that became operational but was not transferred from 'Assets Under Construction' to 'Infrastructure'; £2.04 million of smallholdings incorrectly classified as 'assets held for sale' rather than operational property; and a £1.415 million revaluation error when an asset was moved from 'Held for Sale' to 'Surplus'. All were corrected by management before account finalization, but the pattern indicates control weaknesses in capital asset management processes.
findings.matters: A pattern of material asset misclassifications indicates internal controls over fixed asset management are not sufficiently robust, creating risk of material errors reaching the accounts.
findings.figures: £5.499 million; £2.04 million; £1.415 million
findings.quote: We identified two assets that became operational in 2024-25 but were not transferred from assets under construction to land and buildings until 2025-26. As the values involved were not material, no prior-year adjustment has been made. We also identified a £5.499 million asset (referenced in Appendix 2) that became operational during 2025-26 but had not been accounted for accordingly at the year-end.

findings.headline: Unqualified audit opinion issued on 2025-26 accounts with no uncorrected misstatements
findings.detail: The auditor intends to issue an unqualified opinion confirming the financial statements give a true and fair view and have been properly prepared in accordance with applicable law and UK adopted international accounting standards. No material uncertainties relating to going concern were identified. No misstatements remain uncorrected in the accounts.
findings.matters: For a lender, an unqualified audit opinion is essential assurance that the accounts can be relied upon for financial assessment.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: We intend to issue an unqualified opinion on the accounts.

findings.headline: Commissioning assurance framework still not established, six months after implementation deadline
findings.detail: Three audit recommendations on commissioning arrangements (establishing a commissioning framework, ensuring compliance with it, and reviewing its effectiveness) all targeted 31 March 2026 and remain open as of 25 September 2026. The council is working with the Welsh Local Government Association to develop a shared approach, but has not yet established its own arrangements to assure value for money in commissioning decisions or monitor compliance with commissioning principles.
findings.matters: Councils typically commit significant resources to commissioned and contracted services; without governance arrangements to assure value for money, the council cannot demonstrate effective stewardship of public spending in this material area.
findings.figures: Three recommendations all targeted 31 March 2026; still open 25 September 2026 (six months overdue)
findings.quote: Engagement across Wales has been slower than anticipated and there is no single commissioning model that can simply be adopted across Wales.

findings.headline: US-Iran conflict creating potential material cost pressures on capital programme delivery
findings.detail: The council explicitly flags that ongoing geopolitical conflict is causing disruptions to global energy markets, shipping routes and supply chains. The report notes this could materially increase capital scheme costs through elevated fuel, transport and materials prices, as well as creating risks around scheme completion timescales. The council states it is monitoring and will act where necessary, but has not yet quantified actual impacts.
findings.matters: External cost pressures could materially increase the total cost of delivering the £160.52m capital programme, affecting borrowing needs and cash management; affects both near-term scheme delivery and forward financial planning.
findings.figures: None quantified; conflict ongoing as at report date 30 June 2026
findings.quote: Since the end of February, the conflict between the United States and Iran is already causing major disruptions to global energy markets, shipping routes, and wider supply chains, all of which may have implications for the Council and schemes in the capital programme. Higher fuel, transport, and materials costs could increase the overall price of delivering schemes, while an increase in interest rates will make it more expensive for the Council to borrow to fund its Capital Expenditure.

findings.headline: Council deliberately maintaining short-term borrowing profile to preserve flexibility for refinancing if interest rates fall as forecast
findings.detail: The council is deliberately avoiding long-term fixed-rate borrowing and instead managing debt on a rolling short-term basis. This reflects forecast that PWLB rates will remain at or decline from 3.75% through 2026-27 and into 2028. £56.5m of borrowing is due for repayment in Q2 (£17.5m PWLB, £39m short-term), requiring active refinancing management. The strategy trades immediate rate certainty for future optionality.
findings.matters: Creates refinancing risk if rates rise unexpectedly; indicates council judges rates likely to fall but exposes it to rollover risk and potential liquidity pressure if funding markets tighten.
findings.figures: Q1 2026 repayments: £2m PWLB and £15m short-term; Q1 2026 borrowing taken: £13m short-term; Q2 2026 due repayments: £17.5m PWLB and £39m short-term; Bank Rate at 3.75% since 18 December 2025
findings.quote: Given the current economic uncertainty and as highlighted by MUFG Corporate Markets in Appendix A, it is expected that borrowing rates will decrease over the coming years. Therefore, it is important for the council to avoid committing to long-term high-rate borrowing, thereby maintaining flexibility to take advantage of potential rate reductions.

findings.headline: Capital programme uplifted to £160.52m, requiring £78.3m (48.8%) to be financed by borrowing
findings.detail: The council's capital programme has been increased from the original £128.96m budget to £160.52m, a £31.6m uplift driven by additional grants from Welsh Government and reprofiling between years. With £78.3m expected to be financed through borrowing (against £73.7m prudential and £4.6m supported borrowing), this represents a substantial and sustained borrowing requirement over the forecast period.
findings.matters: Large borrowing needs drive interest costs and debt service obligations; the scale and duration of borrowing determine the council's leverage and interest rate exposure.
findings.figures: Revised capital programme budget 30 June 2026: £160.52m (original £128.96m); borrowing requirement £78.3m (48.8%); Q1 actual spend £4.83m (3% of budget); HRA borrowing £34.86m; general fund borrowing £38.88m
findings.quote: The revised programme at the 30 th June 2026 is budgeted at £160.52 million following the successful award of additional grants and the reprofiling of budgets between financial years.

findings.headline: Aged sundry debt increased by £2.12m to £17.63m, with 74% in difficult-to-collect social care debt
findings.detail: Overdue debt (outstanding more than 30 days) has risen by £2.12m in the quarter to £17.63m. Of this, £13.39m (74%) relates to adult social care fees, which are inherently difficult to collect due to Welsh Government restrictions on bailiff use and the vulnerable circumstances of clients. The increase has been exacerbated by delays in the new finance system implementation affecting invoice allocation and raising.
findings.matters: Aged debt directly impacts cash flow and working capital management; high social care debt is structurally difficult to collect; growth in Q1 suggests a trend that may persist through the year despite mitigations.
findings.figures: Total aged debt (over 30 days) £17.63m, increased by £2.12m since previous quarter; social care debt £13.39m representing 74% of aged debt; total outstanding debt (current and aged) £21.27m representing 25% of annual generated income
findings.quote: The volume of aged debt, defined as amounts outstanding for more than 30 days, totals £17.63 million, this has increased by £2.12 million since the last report. This has not been helped by the implementation of the new finance system which has delayed some payments being allocated to outstanding invoices and delayed some invoices being raised which is resulting in being outstanding for longer.

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement revised down across all forecast years due to additional grants and scheme reprofiling
findings.detail: The council's CFR (a gauge of indebtedness) has been revised lower than budgeted in the original capital strategy. Opening actual CFR is £453.34m versus £467.25m budgeted. The revised estimates for 2026/27 through 2028/29 are £4.3m-£4.7m lower than original forecasts. The reduction reflects additional grants received and the reprofiling of capital schemes into future years, which defers (rather than eliminates) borrowing needs but reduces current-year financing costs.
findings.matters: CFR is the primary measure of a council's indebtedness and determines future borrowing needs; a lower near-term profile improves debt trajectory and reduces immediate financing pressure, though the underlying borrowing requirement remains.
findings.figures: Opening Balance 1st April 2026 Actual 453.34m vs Original Estimates 467.25m; Closing Balance 31st March 2027 Quarter 1 Estimate 525.55m vs Original Estimates 529.85m; Closing Balance 31st March 2028 Quarter 1 Estimate 623.29m vs Original Estimates 627.72m; Closing Balance 31st March 2029 Quarter 1 Estimate 709.09m vs Original Estimates 713.80m

findings.paper_title: GAC Panel Performance Assessment_Process and Organisational Response 25.09.26
findings.headline: Panel recommends the council accelerate its transformation portfolio to deliver defined financial benefits, implying current pace of change is insufficient.
findings.detail: Recommendation 2 directs the council to 'accelerates its transformation portfolio' as part of establishing the financial benefits framework. The use of 'accelerates' suggests the Panel considered the current pace of transformation to be slower than required to meet the council's MTFS assumptions. The Council's response notes it 'has established a transformation portfolio aligned to its Medium-Term Financial Strategy' but must now strengthen 'benefits realisation arrangements and ensure a clear line of sight between transformation activity, impact, financial savings targets and the delivery of sustainable long-term outcomes,' with completion by March 2027.
findings.matters: The pace of transformation activity directly affects the timing and realization of assumed budget savings. If transformation is not accelerating as planned, there is a timing risk to the council's ability to deliver MTFS savings targets on schedule.
findings.figures: March 2027 target completion date for benefits realization framework
findings.quote: accelerates its transformation portfolio and establishes a clear, robust framework linking the MTFS funding target to defined, measurable and realised financial benefits

findings.paper_title: GAC Panel Performance Assessment_Process and Organisational Response 25.09.26
findings.headline: Independent Panel Performance Assessment concluded council is fulfilling its statutory performance duties despite challenging economic and fiscal context.
findings.detail: The Panel's overall finding (Section 3.1 and 4.1) is that 'The Local Authority is fulfilling its performance duties under the Local Government and Elections (Wales) Act 2021,' noting that this assessment was reached 'while recognising that the Council is operating within a challenging economic and fiscal context shared by councils across Wales.' The Panel also noted 'evidence of growing momentum in key areas' and identified 'governance and management arrangements that are sufficiently robust to maintain organisational grip and support continued improvement.'
findings.matters: An independent external assessment that a council is meeting its performance and governance duties—particularly one that acknowledges the challenging context while confirming the council is managing effectively—provides assurance to external stakeholders including lenders that the council has the management capability to navigate financial pressures.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: The Local Authority is fulfilling its performance duties under the Local Government and Elections (Wales) Act 2021.

findings.paper_title: GAC Panel Performance Assessment_Process and Organisational Response 25.09.26
findings.headline: Panel found council is meeting statutory performance duties but identified a governance gap in tracking transformation savings against MTFS targets.
findings.detail: The Panel confirmed that Powys is exercising its functions effectively and maintaining effective governance, but Recommendation 2 specifically requires the council to establish 'a clear, robust framework linking the MTFS funding target to defined, measurable and realised financial benefits, with savings explicitly tracked, accounted for and reported.' This indicates the council's transformation portfolio has savings assumptions in its Medium-Term Financial Strategy that are not currently subject to clear benefit realization tracking. The council has accepted this recommendation and committed to deliver a benefits realization framework and stronger alignment between transformation activity and MTFS by March 2027.
findings.matters: If a council's MTFS assumes transformation savings are being realized but lacks a framework to track whether those savings are actually delivered, it creates uncertainty about the financial sustainability of its budget plan—a direct concern for a lender assessing the council's ability to balance its budget.
findings.figures: MTFS funding target referenced but no specific savings figures disclosed in the paper; target completion March 2027
findings.quote: establishes a clear, robust framework linking the MTFS funding target to defined, measurable and realised financial benefits, with savings explicitly tracked, accounted for and reported

findings.headline: External audit flagged concerns about council meeting tighter future statutory deadlines
findings.detail: While Audit Wales issued an unqualified opinion on 2024-25 accounts and found no significant issues, the auditor included 'some considerations for the Council to consider when delivering future years financial statements within the shorter statutory deadlines.' This signals potential delivery risk as audit deadlines tighten.
findings.matters: An external audit caveat about meeting statutory timelines is a leading indicator of potential future audit delays or qualification risk. Tighter deadlines increase risk of non-compliance.
findings.figures: Draft accounts prepared on time (30 June 2025); unqualified opinion issued in advance of statutory deadline (31 October 2025)
findings.quote: There were no other significant issues to report but they did include some considerations for the Council to consider when delivering future years financial statements within the shorter statutory deadlines.

findings.headline: Whistleblowing policy review missed January 2026 deadline; investigations from December 2024 remain open
findings.detail: The Whistleblowing Policy was reviewed but not presented to Governance and Audit Committee in January 2026 as planned; it was later submitted in May 2026. Three whistleblowing investigations were not complete as of January 2026, with two having been received in December 2024 and one in March 2025.
findings.matters: A missed governance process deadline signals resource or priority pressure. Whistleblowing investigations overdue by 1-4 months delay staff protection mechanisms and issue resolution.
findings.figures: Investigations pending: 3 as of January 2026 (from December 2024 and March 2025)
findings.quote: The Whistleblowing Policy was reviewed but was not presented to the January 2026 Governance and Audit Committee as planned.

findings.headline: Multi-year budget sustainability not yet demonstrated; only 2026-27 balanced
findings.detail: The Financial Management Code assessment for 2025-26 notes the council 'only achieved a balanced budget in 2026-27'. The associated stakeholder feedback action (FMC2) is marked 'Off Track' with the note that it 'should be initiated when the new financial system is embedded', suggesting wider financial planning remains incomplete.
findings.matters: Council can demonstrate only a single year of balanced budget. Multi-year financial sustainability beyond 2026-27 remains unproven, creating refinancing and planning risk.
findings.figures: Balanced budget achieved for 2026-27 only; FMC2 (Wider stakeholder feedback) status: Off Track
findings.quote: Only achieved a balanced budget in 2026-27 but future years' FRM more robust.

findings.headline: Internal audit Limited Assurance opinions increased and fundamental risk actions rose
findings.detail: Limited Assurance audit opinions rose from 6 to 10 (23% to 27% of reviews). Priority 1 (Fundamental) actions requiring immediate attention increased from 8 to 11 (4.4% to 5.5% of all actions). This indicates more control failures and more fundamental risks being identified.
findings.matters: An increase in Limited Assurance opinions signals more control weaknesses in core services. Growth in Priority 1 actions indicates fundamental governance risks requiring urgent remediation.
findings.quote: identified some issues, non-compliance or scope for improvement which may put at risk the achievement of objectives.

findings.headline: Three governance principles downgraded from Substantial to Reasonable assurance
findings.detail: Principles D (Determining interventions to achieve outcomes), E (Developing organisational capacity and leadership), and F (Managing risks and public financial management) all declined by one assurance level from 2024-25 to 2025-26. The council notes that while progress continues, evidence at year end did not support Substantial assurance for these principles.
findings.matters: A simultaneous decline across three principles, especially F covering risk management and financial control, signals governance pressure in core areas. Lenders monitor governance trends as leading indicators of operational stress.
findings.figures: Principle D: Substantial (2024-25) → Reasonable (2025-26); Principle E: Substantial (2024-25) → Reasonable (2025-26); Principle F: Substantial (2024-25) → Reasonable (2025-26)
findings.quote: For Principles B to F, the Council has continued to make ongoing positive progress and has delivered a range of improvements to strengthen governance arrangements. However, while the direction of travel remains positive, the evidence available at year end does not yet provide sufficient assurance to assess these principles as 'substantial'.

findings.paper_title: Council Tax Premiums - Impact Assessment Longterm Empty Properties
findings.headline: Four out of five empty property owners don't believe the stepped premium will work; most cite uninhabitable properties requiring renovation (39.3%)
findings.detail: Consultation found 80.7% of empty property owners 'did not believe a stepped premium would encourage properties to return to use earlier.' The most cited reason for vacancy was properties 'uninhabitable and undergoing or requiring renovation' (39.3%), suggesting financial constraints rather than profit motives. This stakeholder skepticism increases risks of non-payment, avoidance behaviour, and appeals.
findings.matters: If property owners view the premium as ineffective and unaffordable, they are more likely to resist payment or pursue appeals, threatening income collection and increasing administration burden.
findings.figures: 80.7% of property owners don't believe stepped premium will work; 39.3% cite uninhabitable/renovation; 897 properties subject to premium
findings.quote: Most participating property owners did not consider a stepped premium an effective incentive. Among respondents who owned a long-term empty property, 80.7% did not believe a stepped premium would encourage properties to return to use earlier. The most frequently selected reason for a property being empty was that it was uninhabitable and undergoing or requiring renovation, at 39.3%.

findings.paper_title: Council Tax Premiums - Impact Assessment Longterm Empty Properties
findings.headline: Policy objective of bringing empty properties back into use will mechanically reduce future premium income; assessed as highly likely (likelihood 4 of 4)
findings.detail: Risk 4 identifies a fundamental contradiction: the policy's primary objective is to bring empty properties back into use, but if successful, the number of properties liable for premium will fall, reducing future income. The council rates this highly likely (4/4). The income forecast implicitly relies on only partial success in returning properties to use.
findings.matters: This creates an unusual built-in tension between policy objective and financial sustainability; the revenue forecast depends on the policy failing to fully achieve its housing goals.
findings.figures: 897 properties currently subject to premium; likelihood 4, impact 3 (residual: likelihood 3, impact 2)
findings.quote: If the policy is successful, the number of properties liable for the premium will reduce, resulting in lower levels of future premium income and reducing the funding available to support housing initiatives and administration of the scheme.

findings.paper_title: Council Tax Premiums - Impact Assessment Longterm Empty Properties
findings.headline: Collection rates on empty properties already lower than standard; increased premium expected to worsen bad debt (likelihood rated 4 of 4, impact 3 of 4)
findings.detail: The council's own Risk 1 assessment identifies that collection rates on long-term empty properties already trail standard accounts. The council rates it highly likely (4/4) that a higher premium will 'result in a further deterioration in collection rates' and increase accounts entering arrears, requiring recovery action and enforcement. This will reduce the projected additional income and increase collection costs.
findings.matters: If collection rates fall materially on an already-weak customer base, the projected £8.9m additional income will not be realized, and enforcement resource and bad debt will rise.
findings.figures: Likelihood 4, impact 3 (residual: likelihood 3, impact 2); 897 properties liable; 1.3% of 67,445 domestic properties
findings.quote: The Council has already experienced lower collection rates on long-term empty properties than on standard Council Tax accounts and a higher premium may increase the number of accounts entering arrears, requiring recovery action, enforcement activity and legal proceedings.

findings.paper_title: Council Tax Premiums - Impact Assessment Longterm Empty Properties
findings.headline: Council Tax premium income projected at £8.9m over six years, declining from £1.7m to £1.3m annually
findings.detail: Powys proposes increasing Council Tax premiums on long-term empty properties to 200% after 5 years and 300% after 10 years. Income is projected at £1.7m in 2026-27, declining to £1.275m in 2031+, totaling £8.925m gross. After £0.925m in implementation costs, net income is £8m. The annual decline is built into the projection and factors for collection rates and property return to use.
findings.matters: This is material additional recurring income for the council's five-year financial strategy, but the built-in annual decline and high-likelihood risks to collection threaten full realization.
findings.quote: Additional council tax income, factored for collection rate and reduction in long-term empty properties at 2027-28 prices £1.700m £1.615m £1.530m £1.445m £1.360m £1.275m £8.925m

findings.headline: Leisure service has long-term sustainability issues requiring interim capital investment options to be considered by Cabinet.
findings.detail: The Community Wellbeing service reports on Q1 improvements to leisure facilities. However, a separate Cabinet report provides an update on long-term sustainability of the leisure service, outlines key risks and developments since the Leisure Review was paused in 2024, and presents interim capital investment options for consideration. This signals that underlying strategic issues exist beyond immediate Q1 capital spend.
findings.matters: The council's leisure service may require significant capital and/or revenue investment or restructuring; if sustainability is at risk, this could affect future capital plans or revenue budgets.
findings.figures: Leisure Review paused in 2024; separate Cabinet report being prepared
findings.quote: Alongside the delivery of these projects, a separate report has been prepared for Cabinet which provides an update on the long-term sustainability of the leisure service, outlines key risks and developments since the Leisure Review was paused in 2024, and presents interim capital investment options for consideration.

findings.headline: Multiple major education capital schemes are proceeding but at different stages of readiness and with extended delivery timescales.
findings.detail: The Education service has several major projects under the Sustainable Communities for Learning Programme. Two are under construction: Brynllywarch Hall expected completion Summer 2027, Sennybridge expected October 2027. Others are at earlier stages: Ysgol Golwg Pen y Fan has contractor appointed with RIBA 2 expected September 2026; Ysgol Calon Cymru RIBA 2 expected November; Ysgol Bro Epynt at initial design seeking contractor EOI for early 2027; Ysgol Bro Hyddgen and Ysgol Calon y Dderwen at tender preparation. These represent substantial commitments with extended timescales.
findings.matters: Large multi-year projects have delivery and cost risks; delays or cost overruns could impact future years' revenue budgets and borrowing requirements.
findings.figures: Brynllywarch Hall: Summer 2027; Sennybridge: October 2027; other schemes at various stages through 2026-2027
findings.quote: Brynllywarch Hall School Project – construction underway, expected completion Summer 2027; Sennybridge CP School Project – construction underway, expected completion October 2027.

findings.headline: Montgomery Canal project is delayed over planning issues with Natural Resources Wales, with a £2m grant claim from Glandwr Cymru due imminently.
findings.detail: The Montgomery Canal is in final stages (Williams Bridge and Vyrnwy Reserve). The council states the project has been delayed due to issues with NRW in the planning stages, but describes this as in hand. A claim for £2m is due imminently from Glandwr Cymru (the Canal and River Trust in Wales), and the council says it will continue to work to mitigate delays and ensure full spend.
findings.matters: A significant grant-funded project is delayed and depends on external body cooperation and receipt of grant; if the project cannot spend in year, it will reprofile and push borrowing needs forward.
findings.figures: £2 million claim expected from Glandwr Cymru
findings.quote: This has been delayed due to issues with NRW in the planning stages, but this is in hand. A claim for £2m is due imminently from Glandwr Cymru (the Canal and River Trust in Wales)

findings.headline: Capital receipts are underpinned by asset sales where only £0.2m has been received against an expected £4m full year target.
findings.detail: Only £0.2 million of capital receipts has been received to date. Sales totalling £1.8 million are agreed but at legal stage. The council expects to achieve £4 million in sales this year. The council acknowledges dependence on assets being declared surplus promptly, buyers coming forward, sales completing in a timely manner, and general market conditions being in its favour.
findings.matters: Capital receipts are a key financing source for the capital programme; if sales falter, the council will need to borrow more than planned, or reprofile schemes.
findings.figures: £0.2 million received; £1.8 million at legal stage; £4 million expected full year
findings.quote: Capital receipts are a fundamental element of our capital financing strategy and maintaining a reasonable stream of capital receipts relies on assets being declared surplus promptly by service areas, buyers coming forward, sales completing in a timely manner and general market conditions being in the Council's favour.

findings.headline: Almost half the capital programme will be financed by borrowing (£78.3 million), creating ongoing revenue costs.
findings.detail: The council expects to finance £78.3 million (48.8%) of the £160.52 million capital programme through prudential borrowing. The interest costs are charged to the revenue account. The council notes it expects this proportion to fall during the year as grants are received and schemes are reprofiled, but this depends on delivery assumptions.
findings.matters: A lender needs to see that borrowing costs are manageable within revenue spending and that assumptions about receipt of grant funding are realistic.
findings.figures: £78.3 million borrowing (48.8% of £160.52 million total)
findings.quote: £78.3 million (48.8%) of the capital programme is expected to be financed by borrowing, the interest cost for this is charged to the revenue account.

findings.headline: Capital spending at only 3% by end of Q1 makes profiling forecasts uncertain.
findings.detail: The council's Section 151 Officer specifically flags that expenditure is low at only 3% of the total annual programme. The officer notes that accurate profiling of schemes is essential to forecast expenditure, the consequential need to borrow and the impact on the revenue budget. This matters because the council cannot yet forecast how much it will actually need to borrow, or what its true revenue impact will be.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence that the council understands its cash requirements and can manage borrowing predictably; imprecise forecasting of capital spend undermines that confidence.
findings.figures: £4.83 million spent of £160.52 million budget (3%)
findings.quote: Expenditure in the first quarter of the year is low at only 3% of the total annual programme. Accurate profiling of schemes is essential to enable us to accurately project expenditure, the consequential need to borrow and the impact on the revenue budget.

findings.headline: School Improvement savings of £353k managed via temporary one-off mitigation only; longer-term solutions still being developed
findings.detail: Of £753k savings target for School Improvement and Learning, £353k (47%) is being managed through 'temporary mitigation in 2026/27' comprising 'in-year budget management measures and the use of one-off opportunities'. The paper states 'Work continues to identify sustainable recurrent solutions to ensure the savings requirement can be delivered on an ongoing basis.' Council is managing the gap this year through temporary measures but has not solved the underlying budget problem, creating risk the shortfall will recur in 2027-28.
findings.matters: One-off solutions are not sustainable; council will face shortfall in future years when one-off opportunities are exhausted, requiring further urgent action
findings.figures: £353k of £753k (47%) using temporary mitigation; £52k of remaining savings not achieved or assured
findings.quote: Of the £753k savings requirement for School Improvement and Learning, £353k is currently proposed to be managed through temporary mitigation in 2026/27. This reflects a combination of in-year budget management measures and the use of one-off opportunities to support the service whilst longer-term proposals are developed and implemented. Work continues to identify sustainable recurrent solutions to ensure the savings requirement can be delivered on an ongoing basis.

findings.headline: Special school demand surge requiring emergency £500k virement with permanent funding still unidentified for 2027-28
findings.detail: Budget includes virement request for £500k from corporate revenue risk budget to fund additional numbers on roll in special schools from September 2026. The paper explicitly states that 'Permanent funding for this pressure will need to be considered through the Council's 2027-28 budget-setting process' alongside projected increases in allocated Individual Development Plans. Indicates the pressure is ongoing, not one-off, but permanent solutions have not been identified.
findings.matters: Unforecasted surge in special educational need that council cannot absorb; temporary fix via risk budget; signals permanent structural cost increase with no identified funding source
findings.figures: £500k emergency virement from risk budget; permanent funding TBD for 2027-28 onwards
findings.quote: A temporary virement of £500,000 from corporate revenue risk budget to fund the additional numbers on roll in Special schools with effect from September 2026 with the permanent funding request to be included within the FRM for 2027-28.

findings.headline: Children's services forecast £0.4m overspend from high-cost out-of-county placements and increasing complexity with limited local provision
findings.detail: Children's Services forecasts £418k overspend at Q1 after assured savings of £1.4m are delivered. The overspend is driven by high-cost out-of-county placements resulting from increasing complexity of need and 'a national shortage of placements'. Increased demand at front door places additional pressure on assessment, intervention and placement budgets. Service has limited ability to reduce costs while meeting statutory duties.
findings.matters: Reflects combination of demographic demand and national market failure (shortage of local placements); council must incur high costs to meet statutory duties; pressures will persist
findings.figures: £418k forecast overspend; £1.419m assured savings not yet delivered
findings.quote: This position is mainly driven by continued pressure from high-cost out-of-county placements, increasing complexity of need, and increased demand at the front door, which is placing additional pressure on assessment, intervention and placement budgets.

findings.headline: Schools collectively in deficit of £3.3m with 23 schools in deficit and 57 in surplus; drawing down reserves
findings.detail: Schools show a collective net deficit of £3.3m: 23 schools in deficit (£7.181m) against 57 in surplus (£3.875m). Schools are forecast to draw £184k from reserves by year end, improved from the original budget submission of £358k but still indicating structural deficit. The paper notes schools with surplus balances are spending down reserves to support current learners rather than maintaining contingency. The council states it will use powers of intervention where recovery plans are not robust.
findings.matters: Collective school deficit indicates systemic funding pressure; reserve drawdown is unsustainable; raises questions about whether funding is adequate or school management is weak
findings.figures: Net collective deficit £3.306m; 23 schools in deficit (£7.181m); 57 in surplus (£3.875m); forecast reserve draw £184k (improved from £358k budget); largest single deficit £6.261m (secondary)
findings.quote: The improvement reflects recovery action being taken by schools where required. All recovery plans will be reviewed in Quarter 2, with appropriate responses provided to schools. The Council will use its powers of intervention where plans are not sufficiently robust to meet the requirements of the Scheme for Financing Schools.

findings.headline: Adult social care overspend of £0.9m driven by domiciliary care demand (+32.5% hours) and complex needs; out-of-county nursing placements at rates exceeding council thresholds
findings.detail: Adult Services forecasts £5.4m overspend at Q1, reducing to £0.9m after delivery of £4.5m assured savings. The overspend is driven by increased domiciliary care demand (hours increased from 9,056 to 12,001 by June 2026), supporting 147 additional people. Nursing placements present acute pressure: providers indicate the Funded Nursing Care rate is insufficient to cover costs, forcing spot purchases out-of-county at premium rates. Mid and north Powys face acute provider shortages.
findings.matters: Demand pressures are largely uncontrollable by the council; out-of-county placements at unaffordable rates indicate market failure; cost pressures will persist unless addressed nationally
findings.figures: £0.885m forecast overspend (after assured savings); domiciliary care hours 9,056→12,001 (+2,944.80, +32.5%); people supported +147 (+24.5%); £4.539m assured savings not yet delivered
findings.quote: The overspend is due to an increase in service demand in Domiciliary care and transfer of clients from the Care Transfer or Referral Form (CROFT) following assessment as well as the full year effect of Neuadd Maldwyn. The increase in demand is significantly driven by the need to address a reduction in delayed transfer of care (DTOC).

findings.headline: Only 4.6% of £15.4m agreed savings delivered by Q1, creating significant risk to full-year budget balance
findings.detail: Of £15.4m total agreed cost reductions for 2026-27 (including £3.4m rolled forward from prior years), only £703k (4.6%) had been delivered by end of June. A further £14.0m (90.8%) are assessed as 'assured' but not yet delivered, while £356k (2.3%) are 'not yet achieved or assured'. The Section 151 Officer notes the low delivery rate is 'of concern'. This contrasts with Q1 2025-26 when 21.5% of savings had been delivered, showing deteriorating delivery rate.
findings.matters: If assured savings do not materialise, the council will breach its balanced budget requirement; early delivery slippage signals execution risk in the savings programme
findings.figures: 4.6% delivered (£703k of £15.428m); 90.8% assured (£14.016m); 2.3% at risk (£356k); Q1 2025-26 comparison: 21.5% delivered
findings.quote: The low level of delivery at this stage presents a risk to the achievement of the Council's overall savings programme.

findings.headline: Cumulative £28.8m funding gap forecast by 2030-31 threatens medium-term financial sustainability
findings.detail: The Medium-Term Financial Strategy shows a funding gap of £9.7m in 2027-28, rising to a cumulative £28.8m gap by 2030-31 as best-case scenario. The Section 151 Officer states that 'the financial pressure we continue to face is likely to outweigh the funding available' and identifies sustainable cost reduction as essential. This structural deficit cannot be closed by efficiency savings alone and indicates fundamental service redesign will be required.
findings.matters: A cumulative deficit of this magnitude over four years indicates potential insolvency without major intervention, raising questions about ability to sustain services or meet borrowing covenants
findings.figures: £9.7m gap 2027-28; £28.8m cumulative gap 2030-31 (best-case scenario)
findings.quote: The Medium-Term Financial Strategy continues to be extremely challenging with a significant budget gap of at least £28.8 million over the next 4 years as the financial pressure we continue to face is likely to outweigh the funding available.

findings.headline: Whistleblowing Policy review delayed four months and three investigations remain pending after extended periods; council identifies this as a governance failure.
findings.detail: The Whistleblowing Policy review was not presented to the Governance and Audit Committee in January 2026 as originally scheduled; submission occurred in May 2026, a four-month delay. Separately, three whistleblowing investigations were incomplete as of January 2026, with two received in December 2024 (more than one month pending) and one in March 2025. The council explicitly identifies this delay as a governance failure occurring during the year.
findings.matters: Effective whistleblowing procedures and timely investigations are foundational to institutional integrity, and delays in both suggest vulnerabilities in the council's capacity or procedures for managing integrity concerns.
findings.figures: 3 investigations pending at January 2026; 2 received December 2024, 1 March 2025; policy review 4 months late
findings.quote: Of the three Whistleblowing investigations that were not yet complete as at January 2026, two had been received in December 2024 and one in March 2025.

findings.headline: External audit issued unqualified opinion on 2024-25 accounts on time with no uncorrected misstatements; auditor flagged considerations for future shortened statutory deadlines.
findings.detail: Audit Wales issued an unqualified (clean) opinion on Powys's 2024-25 audited statement of accounts, delivered in advance of the 31 October 2025 statutory deadline. Draft accounts were submitted on 30 June 2025 and assessed as 'satisfactory'. No uncorrected misstatements were found. However, the auditor included considerations the council should address when delivering future financial statements within newly shortened statutory deadlines.
findings.matters: A clean audit opinion provides important assurance the council's financial position is fairly presented, though the auditor's caveat about future deadline pressures signals the council may need to accelerate financial reporting processes.
findings.figures: Draft submitted 30 June 2025; unqualified opinion issued in advance of 31 October 2025 deadline; zero uncorrected misstatements
findings.quote: The Auditor issued an unqualified opinion on the accounts in advance of the statutory deadline of 31 October 2025. There were no uncorrected misstatements in the accounts.

findings.headline: New financial system implemented 1 April 2026 at financial year-end, creating embedding risk during a period of governance vulnerabilities.
findings.detail: Powys implemented a new live finance system on 1 April 2026—coinciding with the start of 2026-27 and immediately following a year in which governance assurance levels were downgraded. Implementation was completed on schedule with training and testing undertaken, but the council identifies embedding as an ongoing priority through 30 June 2027. Major financial system changes create inherent control environment risk during transition including staff familiarisation, report development and operational functionality verification.
findings.matters: Major financial system implementations create material control environment risk during embedding, and this transition coincides with the council's recently downgraded governance assurance levels, creating a compounded vulnerability period.
findings.figures: Implementation: 1 April 2026; embedding period to 30 June 2027
findings.quote: New live finance system from 01 April 2026 - embedding processes and reporting

findings.headline: Council achieved balanced budget for 2026-27 only; financial sustainability beyond one year remains undemonstrated.
findings.detail: The council's Financial Management Code assessment records: 'Only achieved a balanced budget in 2026-27 but future years' FRM more robust.' While five-year budget planning was undertaken, the council can only demonstrate a balanced budget position one year ahead. The broader governance forward-look identifies financial sustainability as a risk area expected to be prominent in future actions, indicating unresolved structural pressures.
findings.matters: A council unable to demonstrate multi-year budget balance presents heightened financial sustainability risk to a lender, suggesting structural budget challenges that undermine medium-term financial predictability.
findings.figures: Balanced budget: 2026-27 only; five-year planning undertaken but balance not demonstrated beyond 2026-27
findings.quote: Only achieved a balanced budget in 2026-27 but future years' FRM more robust.

findings.headline: Audit Wales identified 17 significant recommendations split between cyber security (9) and governance review (8); cyber security audit marked Confidential.
findings.detail: The Cyber Security audit by Audit Wales generated 9 recommendations—the highest count of any single regulatory review undertaken during the year and marked Confidential. A separate full governance review identified 8 recommendations on keeping corporate documentation current, forward work programming, report timeliness, and monitoring of service change impact. All recommendations have been accepted; 3 of the 8 governance recommendations implemented with 5 outstanding to March 2027.
findings.matters: Material cyber security gaps and governance audit findings on documentation, reporting and decision-making oversight pose risks to operational resilience and financial system integrity, matters a lender would assess when evaluating institutional capability.
findings.figures: 9 cyber security recommendations; 8 governance review recommendations (3 implemented, 5 outstanding); 17 major recommendations total from external audit
findings.quote: Audit Wales Cyber Security (Confidential) 9

findings.headline: Internal audit findings deteriorated: Substantial Assurance opinions fell from 7.69% to 2.7%, while Limited Assurance opinions rose to 27% of audited areas.
findings.detail: Only 1 internal audit received Substantial Assurance in 2025-26 (2.7%), compared to 2 in 2024-25 (7.69%); a marked decline. Limited Assurance opinions increased from 6 audits (23.08%) to 10 audits (27.0%), indicating emerging control weaknesses across multiple operational areas. The overall Internal Audit opinion remains Reasonable, though with identified issues and scope for improvement noted.
findings.matters: Deteriorating internal audit assurance levels indicate emerging operational control gaps that threaten the council's ability to safeguard resources and maintain reliable financial reporting, matters material to lender confidence.
findings.figures: Substantial Assurance: 2 (7.69%) in 2024-25, 1 (2.7%) in 2025-26; Limited Assurance: 6 (23.08%) in 2024-25, 10 (27.0%) in 2025-26
findings.quote:
Substantial Assurance 2 7.69% 1 2.7%
Limited Assurance 6 23.08% 10 27.0%

findings.headline: Three core governance principles downgraded from 'Substantial' to 'Reasonable' assurance, including Principle F on financial management and internal control.
findings.detail: Principle F, covering managing risks and performance through robust internal control and strong public financial management, was rated Substantial in 2024-25 but dropped to Reasonable for 2025-26. Principles D (determining interventions to optimise outcomes) and E (developing organisational capacity and leadership) were also downgraded. The council states the direction of travel remains positive but evidence at year end did not provide sufficient assurance to sustain Substantial ratings.
findings.matters: A council's assessment that its financial management and internal control framework can no longer sustain Substantial assurance indicates emerging vulnerabilities in systems supporting accurate financial reporting and effective resource management, material to any lender evaluating institutional resilience.
findings.figures: Principle F: Substantial (2024-25) → Reasonable (2025-26); Principles D and E: also Substantial → Reasonable
findings.quote: Substantial assurance continues to be demonstrated for Principles A and G. For Principles B to F, the Council has continued to make ongoing positive progress and has delivered a range of improvements to strengthen governance arrangements. However, while the direction of travel remains positive, the evidence available at year end does not yet provide sufficient assurance to assess these principles as 'substantial'.

findings.paper_title: Report Council Tax Premium Long-term empty properties
findings.headline: The Section 151 Officer supports the proposal from a financial perspective, but with explicit recognition of downside risk.
findings.detail: The Director of Corporate Services confirms 'The recommendations can be supported from a financial perspective' and that the new income 'can be fully funded from the additional income generated'. However, this support is made conditional on the statement that successful implementation will reduce future income from the scheme.
findings.matters: Alignment with the council's chief financial officer is a governance strength, but the caveat signals this is a managed risk rather than unqualified endorsement of the revenue assumption.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: The recommendations can be supported from a financial perspective, recognising that successful implementation should reduce the number of long-term empty properties over time and may therefore reduce future income generated from premiums.

findings.paper_title: Report Council Tax Premium Long-term empty properties
findings.headline: Revenue is explicitly expected to decline if the policy achieves its primary objective of returning empty properties to occupied use.
findings.detail: The paper measures success by reduction in empty properties, not revenue generation. A 5% annual reduction in numbers (consistent with trends after the previous premium increase) would reduce revenue by approximately £80,000 per annum. The S151 Officer notes that 'successful implementation should reduce the number of long-term empty properties over time and may therefore reduce future income generated from premiums'.
findings.matters: A finance director budgeting for £1.5 million must account for significant volatility: the income projection rests partly on the policy not achieving its stated objective, creating conflict between policy success and revenue stability.
findings.figures: 5% annual reduction in empty properties = approximately £80,000 per annum reduction in premium income
findings.quote: successful implementation is expected to reduce the number of properties subject to the premium over time and therefore reduce the level of income generated.

findings.paper_title: Report Council Tax Premium Long-term empty properties
findings.headline: Additional revenue of £1.5 million per annum is projected from a revenue source that consistently collects at a significantly lower rate than standard council tax.
findings.detail: The incremental premium is projected to generate £1.73 million gross, or £1.47 million accounting for 85% collection. However, the paper explicitly states that collection rates on empty property premiums are substantially lower than standard council tax (86% versus 96% in 2025/26). The report flags that 'Increasing the premium charge above 100%, poses a further risk to the in-year collection rate', acknowledging this will worsen.
findings.matters: A lender assessing creditworthiness must account for collection risk, especially where that risk is identified as likely to increase with the policy change.

findings.headline: Overall governance framework stable at 'Reasonable' with no audit qualifications reported
findings.detail: The council's overall governance assurance level remains at Reasonable for the fourth consecutive year (2022/23 through 2025/26). Governance and Audit Committee reviewed the draft statement on 26 June 2026 and made no recommendations. Audit Wales reviewed the draft in July 2026; their observations were incorporated into the final statement. No audit qualifications or material findings are reported.
findings.matters: Absence of audit qualifications and consistent governance assurance indicates the council's internal control environment is functioning without material defects, though the Reasonable level (not Substantial) indicates room for process improvement.
findings.figures: Overall assurance level Reasonable for all four years 2022/23-2025/26
findings.quote: An overall assurance rating of 'Reasonable' was given, meaning that generally, risks are well managed, but some processes could be improved.

findings.headline: Financial management and risk control assurance at 'Reasonable' level, downgraded from 'Substantial' in 2023-24
findings.detail: Principle F, which covers "Managing risks and performance through robust internal control and strong public financial management," is rated at Reasonable for 2025-26 (same as 2024-25). This represents a downgrade from the Substantial rating achieved in 2023-24. Reasonable assurance is defined as "generally, risks are well managed, but some processes could be improved."
findings.matters: Financial management assurance is the governance principle most directly relevant to a lender's credit assessment of the council's financial control environment and operational risk.
findings.figures: Principle F: 2023-24 Substantial, 2024-25 Reasonable, 2025-26 Reasonable
findings.quote: Principle F: Managing risks and performance through robust internal control and strong public financial Management

findings.headline: Housing adaptations service constrained by limited budget despite adding extra resource to clear backlog
findings.detail: Disabled facilities grants and adaptations (measure 337) are running at 69% of target with 100% the goal. The council reports backlog in North area reduced from 90+ to 45 medium/large jobs and has added extra resource, but explicitly identifies budget as the binding constraint preventing target achievement. South area is also reviewing process delays.
findings.matters: A statutory service unable to meet its targets due to budget limitations rather than operational failure suggests either insufficient allocation for housing functions or structural demand exceeding available resources—material to a lender assessing council financial position
findings.figures: 69% actual vs 100% target (measure 337); North backlog 90+ reduced to 45; council expects targets to be met once backlog reaches 20
findings.quote: extra resource has been added to reduce volume but there is still a lot of work to do and limited budget to really make a substantial difference to hit the targets

findings.headline: General Fund reserve stands at exactly the 4% policy minimum (£12.3 million) with no buffer, while the council remains under-borrowed and borrowing costs have risen
findings.detail: Powys's General Fund reserve is £12.3 million, which equals 4.3% of the net revenue budget — the council's stated minimum threshold. While the council notes the reserve has increased by £0.8 million, this increase reflects only a larger revenue base, leaving no safety buffer above policy minimum. Simultaneously, the council 'remains under-borrowed as we continue to utilise our cash reserves to underpin our cashflow' but notes 'the cost of borrowing has risen.' This creates a timing trap: as reserves approach or fall below minimum (schools are already drawing £186k), the council will need to move to borrowing at higher cost.
findings.matters: A council with reserves at minimum policy level has no flexibility for unexpected pressures or funding reductions. Any further deterioration will breach reserves policy and trigger external intervention. Combined with the £28.8m medium-term gap, this signals the council is approaching the edge of its financial envelope. For lenders, reserves at minimum + rising borrowing costs + medium-term deficit = refinancing risk.
findings.figures: General Fund reserve £12.3m (4.3% of net revenue budget); minimum policy level 4%; reserve increase from prior year £0.8m
findings.quote: The Council remains under-borrowed as we continue to utilise our cash reserves to underpin our cashflow. We can borrow both in the short to medium or longer term, but the cost of borrowing has risen.

findings.headline: The council faces a £9.7 million funding gap in 2027-28 and a cumulative £28.8 million gap through 2030-31, with the Section 151 Officer warning that financial pressure will 'outweigh the funding available'
findings.detail: Powys's Medium-Term Financial Strategy identifies a funding gap of £9.7 million for 2027-28 and a cumulative gap of £28.8 million through 2030-31 'as a best-case scenario.' The Section 151 Officer has stated: 'Our Medium Term Financial Strategy continues to be extremely challenging with a significant budget gap of at least £28.8 million over the next 4 years as the financial pressure we continue to face is likely to outweigh the funding available.' No solution to this gap is yet identified; the officer notes that 'work on the development of proposals for 2027-28 to 2031-32 is already underway', signalling no quick fix exists.
findings.matters: A cumulative £28.8 million gap over four years, with no identified solution, is a sustainability crisis. This is not a single-year pressure or a technical forecast adjustment — it is a statement that the council's spending trajectory is unsustainable relative to funding. For lenders, this signals potential default risk in the medium term unless dramatic service cuts or spending cuts occur.
findings.figures: 2027-28 funding gap £9.7m; cumulative gap through 2030-31 £28.8m (best-case)
findings.quote: The MTFS published alongside the budget in February shows a funding gap of £9.7 million in 2027-28 and a cumulative funding gap by 2030-31 estimated at £28.8 million as a best-case scenario.

findings.headline: 23 schools are in financial deficit including one secondary with a £6.5 million projected deficit, and schools collectively are drawing £186k from reserves instead of building them
findings.detail: At Q1, 23 schools are projected to end the year in deficit (7 secondary schools, 13 primary, 2 all-age, 1 special), with a combined projected deficit of £7.181 million. One secondary school alone projects a deficit of £6.510 million. Rather than contributing to reserves, schools are expected to draw £186k from reserves by year-end (against a budgeted £2k contribution). While the council notes this is 'significantly improved' from the original budget submissions (which projected £358k draw), it still signals schools are collectively spending faster than they are funded. The council has created specific virements to clear accumulated deficits at Crickhowell High School (£374k for sports facilities, £68k for library).
findings.matters: Multiple schools in persistent deficit is a governance failure. A single secondary school deficit of £6.5m is a crisis-level problem for a council that must intervene. For lenders, schools deficits signal either underfunding in the formula, poor cost control, or both — and they consume council reserves and management time.
findings.figures: 23 schools in deficit; secondary school deficit of £6.510m; total school deficit of £7.181m; projected year-end reserve draw £186k; virements to clear Crickhowell deficits: £374k + £68k
findings.quote: Schools are collectively budgeting a £2k contribution to reserves, but at Quarter 1 a further projected draw of reserves of £186k is now expected by year end on 31 March 2027.

findings.headline: Children's Services is £418k overspent and facing a national shortage of placements driving up costs faster than the council can manage demand
findings.detail: Children's Services is forecasting a £418k overspend at Q1 due to 'continued pressure from high-cost out-of-county placements, increasing complexity of need, and increased demand at the front door.' The service explicitly notes 'a national shortage of placements', which is forcing Powys to compete for capacity and accept higher per-placement costs. The service holds £1.419 million of assured savings but acknowledges these remain 'subject to active monitoring' and faces 'demand-led pressures' that are outside its control.
findings.matters: Like Adult Services, this reflects a market problem (national shortage) combined with rising need. The council has limited control over placement availability or cost. For lenders, this is a second high-need, under-funded service showing structural deterioration.
findings.figures: Q1 projected overspend £418k; £1.419m assured cost reductions still at risk
findings.quote: Children's Services is forecasting a £418k projected overspend at end of Quarter 1 based on actuals and forecasted expenditure. This position is mainly driven by continued pressure from high-cost out-of-county placements, increasing complexity of need, and increased demand at the front door, which is placing additional pressure on assessment, intervention and placement budgets.

findings.headline: Adult Services is £5.4 million gross overspend driven by 32% surge in domiciliary care demand and nursing home cost inflation that the council cannot control
findings.detail: Adult Services reported a £5.424 million gross overspend at Q1. Even after assured savings of £4.539 million, the service will run £885k over budget. The driver is structural: domiciliary care hours surged 32% in five months (from 9,056 in April 2025 to 12,001 in June 2026), with people supported jumping from 599 to 746. The service notes that nursing home providers are stating the Funded Nursing Care rate 'is insufficient and does not cover their costs.' This is forcing out-of-county spot purchases 'at increased rates often above the host authority rates', particularly in mid and north Powys where local nursing provision cannot meet demand. The service is managing this year through prevention and repatriation but identifies this as ongoing structural pressure.
findings.matters: This is not a one-year budget blip but an aging-population problem the council cannot close with efficiency alone. Higher care complexity, workforce shortages forcing agency costs, and insufficient FNC rates mean placement costs will keep rising faster than funding. For lenders, this is a high-risk, under-funded service that deteriorates as demographics shift.
findings.figures: Gross overspend £5.424m; domiciliary care hours 9,056 (Apr-25) to 12,001 (Jun-26), +32%; people supported 599 to 746, +24%; net overspend after assured savings £885k (0.8% of £111.7m budget)
findings.quote: The forecast outturn at the end of Quarter 1 (period 3), 30th June 2026, is a £5.424 million overspend. Our ageing population with increased complexity of need is outstripping nursing provision within the county and forcing us to spot purchase out of county placements at increased rates often above the host authority rates.

findings.headline: Only 4.6% of the £15.4 million savings programme has been delivered by quarter 1, with £355k explicitly at risk of non-delivery
findings.detail: The council requires £15.4 million of cost reductions to balance 2026-27, including £3.4 million rolled forward from prior years. By end of Q1, just £0.7 million (4.6%) has actually been delivered. While £14.0 million (90.8%) is assessed as assured, £355k remains unachieved and at risk. The Section 151 Officer has explicitly warned that 'The low level of delivery at this stage presents a risk to the achievement of the Council's overall savings programme.' Services are being challenged to explain slippage and identify mitigation, but this puts the entire 2026-27 balance at risk if the assured pipeline slips.
findings.matters: A council that has delivered 4.6% of a 15-month programme by quarter 1 is not on track. If delivery continues at this rate, two-thirds of savings will slip, and the £2.1m underspend shown here will reverse to a substantial deficit. For lenders, this signals the 2026-27 outturn itself is unreliable.
findings.figures: £0.7m delivered (4.6%); £14.0m assured (90.8%); £355k at risk (2.3%); total programme £15.4m
findings.quote: £0.4 million (2.3%) are described as unachieved and are at risk of delivery in this year. Services are being challenged as to the reasons for the changes in positions for some savings proposals and will be required to consider mitigating action to ensure that they can deliver within the budget allocated.

findings.matters: A £420k (16%) adverse variance within a single year indicates forecasting gaps or unexpected cost pressures. In a system already running structural deficits, this volatility increases risk.
findings.figures: Forecast deficit £2.7m (May 2025); actual deficit £3.1m (March 2026); variance £420k
findings.quote: This position has deteriorated compared to Schools' original budget plans (May 2025) which projected a total deficit balance of £2.7million for 31 March 2026, an increase in deficit of £0.421million against the projections during the financial year.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Report School Outturn Positions 31 March 2026 and Budget Plans 2026-27 FINAL
findings.headline: Schools are not complying with council financial direction; only 59% of schools honoured deficit agreements
findings.detail: The council issued 17 deficit agreements in 2025-26 but only 10 schools complied, leaving 7 in non-compliance. Of 26 schools planning deficits for 2026-27, 20 are classified as 'unlicensed' (outside scheme criteria). Four schools ended the year in deficit that they had not forecast, suggesting either weak budget control or genuine volatility. The council is requiring 9 schools to submit recovery plans and has issued warnings and notices of concern to others.
findings.matters: Low compliance with council financial direction indicates weak governance over delegated budgets. Schools forecasting deficits but not following council process suggests supervisory failures.
findings.figures: 17 deficit agreements issued, 10 complied (59%); 20 unlicensed deficits of 26 projected; 4 schools with unforecasted year-end deficits; 6 warning notices, 2 notices of concern in place
findings.quote: 17 deficit agreements were issued in 2025-26, and 10 schools have complied with these. We have analysed the reasons for non-compliance at the remaining seven schools and appropriate action will be taken where required.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Report School Outturn Positions 31 March 2026 and Budget Plans 2026-27 FINAL
findings.headline: Council can only secure one year of school funding despite deficits; future years described as 'extremely challenging'
findings.detail: The council injected £5.6m additional revenue funding in 2026-27 to fully fund the school budget formula, including £1.8m targeted to secondary phase. However, officers state that finding similar growth in future years 'will be extremely challenging' given the 'difficult public finance environment'. Schools are forecasting deficits extending to 2028-29 and beyond, but the council has not committed funding to cover them.
findings.matters: A one-year funding fix to a multi-year deficit problem signals the council lacks a sustainable solution. Future deficits may force either further council subsidy or deficit budgets for schools.
findings.figures: £5.6m additional investment 2026-27; £1.8m to secondary phase; projected deficit remaining at £7.3m for 2026-27
findings.quote: The funding figures that schools have based their budgets on for 2026-27 includes an additional £5.6 million of revenue investment approved by the Council at budget setting in February 2026, which ensures that the formula is fully funded going forward. Continuing to find the budget growth to allow the schools delegated funding formula to be fully funded in future years for the current schools estate will be extremely challenging

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Report School Outturn Positions 31 March 2026 and Budget Plans 2026-27 FINAL
findings.headline: Secondary schools alone hold £6.2m in cumulative deficit with individual institutions carrying deficits over £1m
findings.detail: The secondary sector deficit of £6.2m dwarfs primary surplus of £2.8m. Five secondary schools carry deficits exceeding £1m: Crickhowell High (£1.4m projected 2026-27), Brecon High (£1.9m), Ysgol Calon Cymru (£1.9m), Llanidloes High (£306k), and Ysgol Maesydderwen (£493k). These are not small schools: Crickhowell serves 931 pupils, Ysgol Calon Cymru 954 pupils.
findings.matters: Secondary deficits are structural, not cyclical, and concentrated in large institutions that are difficult to close. The council's ability to manage these schools financially is questionable.
findings.figures: Secondary sector deficit £6.155m (31 March 2026); Crickhowell High £1.176m (2025-26) forecasted to £1.392m (2026-27); Brecon High £1.948m; Ysgol Calon Cymru £1.984m
findings.quote: Of the budgets submitted, fifty-four schools are budgeting to be in a cumulative surplus position at 31 March 2027... Twenty-six schools are budgeting to be in a cumulative deficit position

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Report School Outturn Positions 31 March 2026 and Budget Plans 2026-27 FINAL
findings.headline: School deficits have more than doubled in six years, reaching £7.6m at March 2026, with no recovery visible
findings.detail: Carried forward school deficits grew from £3.7m (2020) to £7.6m (2026), affecting 31 schools at year-end vs 14 in 2020. The council's actual outturn deficit of £3.1m exceeded the planned £1.6m by £2.0m during 2025-26 alone. For 2026-27, 26 schools are planning to set deficits and the cumulative position is forecast to remain at £7.3m despite £5.6m new council investment.
findings.matters: Persistent school deficits consume council reserves and require ongoing subsidy. The scale and trend suggest structural funding inadequacy across the school system, not temporary fluctuation.
findings.figures: £7.648m deficit (2025-26); £3.1m outturn deficit vs £1.6m budgeted; 31 schools in deficit (vs 14 in 2020); 26 schools planning deficits for 2026-27
findings.quote: At 31 March 2026, the total cumulative reserves for schools (including the balance on the closed schools reserve) was in a deficit position of £3.565million

findings.headline: Performance Panel Assessment underway in April 2026 will assess council effectiveness and governance; outcome and recommendations not yet known.
findings.detail: The council is undertaking its first Performance Panel Assessment between 21-24 April 2026 (Action IA6). The assessment will reflect whether the council is exercising its functions effectively, using resources economically/efficiently, and has effective governance in place. Final report expected in 2026-27.
findings.matters: A regulatory performance panel assessment is underway and may identify additional governance/performance gaps or recommendations beyond those already flagged. The assessment was scheduled for April 2026 and findings will inform 2026-27 priorities.
findings.figures: Performance Panel Assessment dates: 21-24 April 2026.
findings.quote: The Council is undertaking its first Performance Panel Assessment (PPA) between 21 and 24 April 2026... This action will be complete at the beginning of 2026/27, when the assessment takes place.

findings.headline: Information governance: Freedom of Information response compliance was off track, requiring mid-year escalation procedures reintroduction.
findings.detail: Action IA5 (Review the effectiveness of the Council's ability to meet its information request response time obligations) identified underlying staff retention issues in the Information Compliance Team following higher-than-usual turnover. Escalation procedures had to be revised and reintroduced in mid-year to improve service engagement and compliance with statutory timescales.
findings.matters: Deterioration in statutory compliance (FOI response times) due to unexpected staff turnover and the need to reintroduce escalation procedures mid-cycle suggests governance process brittleness and possible HR/retention challenges affecting service resilience.
findings.figures: Higher than usual staff turnover in Information Compliance Team; leaver interviews and analysis conducted.
findings.quote: Work has been undertaken within the Information Compliance Team to better understand retention issues following a higher than usual level of staff turnover... Escalation procedures have been revised and re-implemented for instances where no response is received from services following tasking emails.

findings.headline: Whistleblowing policy review delayed and governance investigations backlog not cleared.
findings.detail: The Whistleblowing Policy was scheduled for Governance and Audit Committee in January 2026 but was not presented then; it was submitted in May 2026. Additionally, three whistleblowing investigations that were not complete as of January 2026 included two that had been open since December 2024 (13 months) and one since March 2025 (10 months).
findings.matters: Delays in establishing and updating whistleblowing procedures, combined with a backlog of unresolved investigations, suggest governance processes are not operating promptly and may indicate resource or management capacity issues that affect overall control environment credibility.
findings.figures: Three whistleblowing investigations: two received December 2024, one received March 2025; status unresolved as of January 2026.
findings.quote: The Whistleblowing Policy was reviewed but was not presented to the January 2026 Governance and Audit Committee as planned... Of the three Whistleblowing investigations that were not yet complete as at January 2026, two had been received in December 2024 and one in March 2025.

findings.headline: Financial sustainability concerns: council achieved balanced budget only for 2026-27, with earlier years showing budget pressure.
findings.detail: Under Financial Management Code action FMC8, the council notes "Only achieved a balanced budget in 2026-27 but future years' FRM more robust. Heads of Service were asked to plan their service delivery and budget requirement over a five-year period, assuming no growth in funding available." This indicates prior-year budget strain and continued cash constraint assumptions.
